pages.text: Ten minutes before Basic 8’s mock digital quiz, every desktop in the ICT room lost connection to the local offline learning server at once! Tracing the dusty skirting board with Uncle Fiifi, Sena found where a mouse had chewed through one shared cable near Door 1. “This old setup used a Bus topology, where all nodes share a single central backbone cable,” Uncle Fiifi explained. “Its biggest weakness is that a single break in the main bus brings the entire Local Area Network (LAN) down! Upgrading to a Star topology gives every computer—and the library block—its own dedicated twisted-pair cable running into a central network switch.”

pages.text: To link the library reading corner to the ICT room’s new central switch, Kobby plotted both buildings on a campus coordinate grid scaled in metres where the Y-axis pointed due North. From the ICT switch at origin I(0, 0), the library terminal L lay 24 metres East and 18 metres North—giving displacement vector IL = (24, 18), which can be written as a column vector with 24 above 18! Using vector magnitude (Pythagoras’ theorem), Kobby found the straight-line distance: |IL| = √(24² + 18²) = √(576 + 324) = √900 = 30 metres. Calculating clockwise from North, Kobby used tan⁻¹(24 ÷ 18) ≈ 53.1°, which rounds to 53°, written as a three-figure bearing: 053°!

pages.text: Hamdia tested Kobby’s BECE geometry with a sharp follow-up question: “If the bearing of the Library from the ICT switch is 053°, what is the back-bearing of the ICT switch from the Library when we sight back along the straight line between the buildings?” Drawing a second North arrow at point L and using alternate interior angles, Kobby added 180° to 053°: “180° + 53° = 233°! Whenever a forward bearing is less than 180°, you add 180° to find the reverse bearing—and you always measure clockwise from North, never from East or South.”

pages.text: Rather than stringing bare Cat6 cable across the sunny courtyard where footsteps, rainwater, and rodents would ruin it—or digging straight through a flowerbed—the team followed the paved L-shaped walkway (24 m East + 18 m North = 42 m along the walls, plus 6 m of vertical cable allowances = 48 m of cable). The wall-mounted conduit covered the 42 m walkway route, while the remaining 6 m allowed for cable drops inside the buildings. Using Career Technology skills, Hamdia planned rigid UV-resistant PVC conduit in 3-metre lengths (42 ÷ 3 = 14 straight pipe lengths, with suitable bends and fittings counted separately), cut square ends cleanly with a fine-toothed junior hacksaw, smoothed burrs with abrasive paper so sharp plastic edges would not scrape cable insulation, and installed suitable inspection bends following the manufacturer’s instructions.

pages.text: Back inside, Uncle Fiifi explained why their Star LAN used a network switch rather than an old hub or a wide-area router alone. “A switch learns the hardware MAC addresses of each computer and learns connected devices’ MAC addresses and normally forwards Ethernet frames to the appropriate port, reducing unnecessary traffic compared with a hub,” he noted. “Later, when the school connects this LAN to the wider internet—a Wide Area Network (WAN)—a router and firewall will sit at the gateway between our switch and the outside world.” Under Uncle Fiifi’s supervision, Sena terminated the low-voltage Ethernet connectors correctly and checked them with a cable tester and clicked each cable into the switch.

pages.text: After the technician checked the installation and powered up the central switch, crisp green link lights blinked across all ports from Lab PC 1 right out to the Library terminal on bearing 053°. Even when Uncle Fiifi unplugged PC 2’s patch cord as a fault test, every other computer and the library catalogue stayed online without a flicker! Labelling each conduit run neatly on their campus network map, the trio saw how Star topology, vector geometry, and protective Career Tech trunking build infrastructure that lasts.

activities.question: Why did upgrading the computer lab to a Star topology make the network more reliable against cable damage?
options: Each node has its own cable to the switch, isolating cable breaks
A Star topology uses zero cables and requires no switch or electricity
A Bus topology continues working faster whenever its main cable is cut

activities.question: The bearing of Library (L) from ICT (I) is 053°. What is the three-figure back-bearing of I from L?
options: 233° (found by adding 180° to 053°, measured clockwise from North at L)
53° (written with two digits and measured anti-clockwise from South)

activities.question: What is the key advantage of a network switch over a simple hub inside a Star LAN?
options: A switch forwards frames to destination ports rather than repeating to all
A switch converts alternating current into plastic conduit pipes
A hub blocks all local computers from communicating with a file server

activities.prompt: Put the campus LAN installation workflow in the correct engineering order.
items: Map building coordinates, compute displacement vector, bearings, and length.
Measure, cut, deburr, and mount protective PVC conduit trunking along walls.
Draw Cat6 data cable through conduit; terminate and test connectors.
Connect node cables into the central switch and test fault isolation.
